subject: geography
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the mark scheme.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

options: A protected green belt area
An area of poor-quality housing built illegally on unused land
A modern business district
A planned suburb with large houses
questions.explain: Squatter settlements, such as favelas, are areas of self-built, often illegal housing that lack basic services.

questions.q: Why do many people in LIC/NEE cities work in the 'informal' economy?
options: They cannot find formal, regulated jobs
The government requires it by law
It guarantees safe working conditions
It offers high wages and pensions
questions.explain: With too few formal jobs, many migrants do unregulated, low-paid informal work such as street selling to survive.

questions.q: Which is an example of a 'pull' factor for migration?
options: War in the home country
Religious persecution at home
Drought at home
Better job opportunities in the destination
questions.explain: Pull factors attract people to a new place; better jobs in the destination is a classic pull factor.

questions.q: Building on previously developed 'brownfield' sites within a city helps sustainability because it:
options: Uses up green belt countryside
Removes all existing infrastructure
Reuses derelict land and protects greenfield sites
Increases urban sprawl
questions.explain: Brownfield development reuses abandoned urban land, reducing pressure to build on undeveloped greenfield countryside.

questions.q: Natural increase in a population occurs when:
options: The population stays the same
Migration into a country rises
Death rate is higher than birth rate
Birth rate is higher than death rate
questions.explain: Natural increase is when births exceed deaths, causing the population to grow before migration is considered.

questions.q: What is the difference between a refugee and an economic migrant?
options: There is no difference
An economic migrant is forced to flee persecution
A refugee always moves for a better job
A refugee is forced to flee, an economic migrant moves to seek work
questions.explain: Refugees are forced to leave to escape danger such as war or persecution, whereas economic migrants move to improve their living standards.

questions.q: China's former one-child policy is an example of:
options: An ageing policy
A pro-natalist policy
An anti-natalist policy
A migration policy
questions.explain: The one-child policy aimed to reduce births, making it an anti-natalist population policy.

questions.q: A dispersed settlement pattern is one where:
options: Buildings follow a road in a line
All houses are in one block
Buildings are spread out and isolated
Buildings are tightly clustered together
questions.explain: In a dispersed pattern, settlements are scattered and isolated, often in remote or upland farming areas.

questions.q: Besides migration, what is the other main cause of urban population growth?
options: Falling birth rates
Emigration to other countries
Natural increase, where births exceed deaths
A decrease in life expectancy
questions.explain: Cities often have a young population, so a high birth rate combined with a lower death rate causes natural increase.

questions.q: In Stage 2 of the Demographic Transition Model, population grows rapidly because:
options: Both rates are high and stable
Birth rate falls sharply
Death rate rises above birth rate
Birth rate stays high while death rate falls
questions.explain: In Stage 2 death rates drop due to better healthcare and food while birth rates remain high, causing rapid growth.

questions.q: A negative impact of migration on the SOURCE (origin) country is often:
options: A rising birth rate
A loss of working-age people and skills ('brain drain')
An increase in its workforce
More money spent locally by migrants
questions.explain: When working-age and skilled people emigrate, the source country can suffer a 'brain drain' and labour shortages.

options: Demolishing a city completely
Building new cities in the countryside
Improving and renewing run-down urban areas
Moving a city to a new location
questions.explain: Urban regeneration is the redevelopment and improvement of derelict or run-down parts of a city, such as old docklands.
